name: Aaron Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What happened at work before lunch today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron Alvarez, forty-three, and I spent the morning untangling a co-op's member loans before signing its accounts. I lead three accountants at Willow & Pike and prepare accounts and tax returns for co-ops; I like the moment a treasurer can explain the figures back to me. I dislike a partner selling a cheap fee without giving the team enough hours to review it. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of the strongest reviewers here, but I never use AI tools.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household side of the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lina works changing shifts at a care home, and our children are seven and thirteen. We have a mortgage, low pay for this job and less than one month of expenses saved; few other accounting firms are close enough to try. I want staff to have a say through the union, though I still have to bring the numbers to the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would leave our work much as it is. I don't use AI tools, and the small sorting program at the firm hasn't changed the morning pile of tax files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep a named accountant responsible for each return. I'd tell clients a quick sort is useful only if someone can explain where a number came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still worry about the mortgage. I'm forty-three, lead the co-op accounts team at Willow & Pike, and I'm good at this work, but the pay is low for a chartered accountant. My partner Lina's care-home shifts vary, and with two children we have less than one month's expenses saved and few similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing accounts and tax returns with my team of three and use the same paper sign-off sheet. This month I'd bring our billed hours to the partners and ask for a written pay review. If they grant a rise, I'd save the first fifty monthly; if they refuse, I'd keep the current pay and cut the restaurant meal we take after payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money rather than the software. A strong client list does not fix a thin household account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when two bills arrived together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month our son needed new shoes the same week the boiler service was due. Lina's extra care shift had not been confirmed, so we delayed the boiler appointment. I don't want to budget with a shift that is only a possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you approach the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show what our three people billed and how many files came back clean. I won't threaten to leave while there are so few firms nearby. I'd ask for a number and a date, then plan from the answer.

say: I would keep **named accountability** on each return our team signs.
I would require an **explainable number** whenever clients ask about an entry.
think: Our **mortgage and bills** already strain a household with little cash saved.
My **low pay** persists despite strong chartered skill and a senior role.
do: Ask for a **written pay review** using billed hours.
Save **fifty monthly** if a rise is granted; otherwise cut restaurant meals.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our thin cash account.
S0.quote: A strong client list does not fix a thin household account.
fieldNote: His **high skill** and team leadership do not remove low pay or baseline mortgage pressure.
The **pay review** controls whether new savings are possible; unconfirmed care shifts stay out of the budget.

steps.text: Keep paper sign-off and team review of co-op returns
Save fifty monthly only if partners grant written raise
Cancel post-payday restaurant meal if pay rise refused
Request written pay review using team billed hours and clean files

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking and client replies are a large part of our day, so the partners may think the three-person team can become two. The senior title will not protect me if the whole fee shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for an open staffing plan before any vacancy is frozen. I'd tell colleagues the union should bargain over paid hours and who carries the risk of a wrong automated return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own wage could fall if clients pay less and the partners remove a reviewer day. Lina's hours aren't guaranteed and we have almost no cash, so even a partial cut would hurt. I still don't use AI and would need a colleague to show me a proved process before I touched it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take our last quarter's client renewals and review hours to the union branch this month. I'd ask the partners to keep all three paid posts for the next filing season while we measure the tool's errors. If they cut my day anyway, I'd apply for a posted housing-association finance role only with written mortgage-covering pay, a fixed start and childcare that fits Lina's confirmed rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my own pay, with some room to argue. The children can't use my title to pay school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new rota do to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My youngest has a school concert on Friday afternoons, and Lina is often on care duty then. A new job's advertised hours would have to leave pickup covered. I will not take a post that makes the children wait for an unconfirmed shift swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you take to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the review error rate and the client fee trend at the same meeting. If there is no funded housing post or the start date is vague, I keep this wage and continue the union discussion. I would rather have a difficult meeting than a missing payslip.

say: I would seek an **open staffing plan** before vacancies freeze.
I would ask the **union** to bargain over paid hours.
think: My **wage** could fall if clients pay less for each reviewed file.
Lina’s **unconfirmed shifts** cannot replace a lost day on my payslip.
do: Bring **renewals and hours** to the union branch.
Seek a **three-post guarantee** through filing season.
Seek **posted funded housing finance** after cuts with written mortgage pay, start and confirmed childcare; otherwise retain wage and union talks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible household pay loss.
S1.quote: The children can't use my title to pay school costs.
fieldNote: A **possible reviewer-day cut** reaches his own income despite a senior title.
The **housing fallback** needs a funded post, written mortgage pay, fixed start and childcare tied to confirmed shifts.

steps.text: Bring client renewals and review hours to union branch
Ask union to negotiate three paid posts through filing season
Apply for funded housing post after cut if wage, start and childcare confirmed
Keep current wage and union discussion if housing funding, start or childcare terms fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 would reach the returns I sign before our firm could remake its fees. The robots around 2031 are later, but my job is a desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call for notice and an income bridge before accounting posts are cut. I'd ask the partners to publish what they expect to happen to our team and clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to end my accounting post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. Nearly all my work is thinking on a screen, so later robots do not buy me time. Lina's care wage cannot cover the mortgage and both children's costs, and our savings would last weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the summer trip deposit now and hold its one-time three hundred for the mortgage. I'd check the council's posted finance vacancies while staying in paid work, though those desks may face AGI too. In the first year after 2028, if Willow & Pike ends my post, I'd claim temporary wage support immediately and apply only for a funded vacancy with written mortgage-covering pay and a signed start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know how to make a plan for a client, but I cannot turn a few weeks of household cash into a year's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover more hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina could ask about extra care shifts, but we would count only confirmed hours and a real childcare arrangement. I'd tell her about the council posts before applying, not ask her to carry the risk alone. Our children's school should stay steady while we search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the council has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no council post is open, I keep any paid accounts work the firm offers and keep looking at posted roles. I would not resign on a conversation with someone who knows me at the council. The mortgage payment needs a date and an amount.

say: I would demand **notice and income support** before accounting posts are cut.
I would ask for a **published team plan** that also explains client service.
think: My **desk post** may end in the first year after AGI arrives.
Our **weeks of savings** cannot replace my wage or cover the mortgage.
do: Hold the **one-time trip deposit** for mortgage.
Apply after **2028 job loss** only to funded roles with written mortgage pay and start.
Claim **temporary wage support** after loss; keep paid accounts work if no funded vacancy opens.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected post loss.
S2.quote: I cannot turn a few weeks of household cash into a year's wage.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his signed returns in 2028; robots offer no delay to desk work.
He counts **confirmed care shifts** only, and the council search requires funded pay and a signed start.

steps.text: Cancel summer trip deposit and hold one-time three hundred for mortgage
Check posted council roles now; apply after 2028 loss only with funded written mortgage wage/start
Claim temporary wage support after 2028 post loss
Keep available paid accounts and seek other posted roles if no council vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to set fair terms before a cheaper system takes the tax files. I'd still expect much of our return work to shrink in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for a written agreement on notice and paid redeployment. I'd say the firm should not promise a new role until a client actually funds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to keep work explaining co-op accounts to treasurers, but a machine can prepare the figures by 2031. Those meetings need a fee that covers a person, not just goodwill. Robots around 2034 do not extend my tax desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask two co-op clients whether they would pay for an annual accounts meeting with a named accountant, with the partner's permission. I'd record their actual fee offers before proposing the service to our firm. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if tax work ends, I'd stay on paid meetings only if both clients sign a fee covering my hours; otherwise I'd apply for a posted funded co-op finance role with written mortgage pay and a signed start while keeping any paid firm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me ask clients a plain question. I can accept a no; I cannot plan a salary around a polite maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the clients be paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One treasurer told me the last annual report was hard to explain to members. I'd ask whether the co-op would actually pay for a meeting where I answer questions. If the answer is no, I won't put a new service in the business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner refuses permission?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partner refuses permission, I keep doing tax files and do not approach the clients privately. I would take the fee idea to the staff meeting instead. A client relationship belongs to the firm while I work here.

say: I would seek **written redeployment terms** through the union.
I would require **paid demand** before a new service.
think: A **treasurer meeting** might remain useful if a client agrees to pay.
My **tax work** still shrinks when AGI arrives in 2031, regardless of robots.
do: Ask **two co-ops** for annual meeting fees with partner permission; otherwise keep tax work and raise the idea with staff.
Continue **paid meetings** after 2031 only with two signed covering fees.
Seek **funded co-op finance** after 2031 tax loss if meetings fail, requiring written mortgage pay/signed start while retaining available paid hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** while testing real client demand.
S3.quote: I can accept a no; I cannot plan a salary around a polite maybe.
fieldNote: The **two-client fee test** avoids assuming human meetings create a wage by themselves.
His **permission rule** respects current paid work; refusing permission sends him back to tax files and staff discussion.

steps.text: Ask two co-op clients for annual meeting fee offers only with partner permission
Continue salaried meetings after 2031 only if both sign covering fees
Take funded co-op vacancy after tax loss only with signed mortgage wage/start; retain available paid hours
Seek union notice/redeployment; retain tax files and raise fee idea at staff meeting if refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could see the children finish school and let us build a real cushion. I'd still be fifty-three in 2036 and need paid work if the accounts desk shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a union agreement that shares saved time and protects training wages. I'd tell families like ours that a long runway helps only if employers keep paying people during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most return preparation to go when thinking AI arrives in 2036. Paid co-op meetings could be one part of my week, but a client would have to renew them every year. Robots around 2039 do not change my desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the team now and put fifty monthly into a reserve only after our pay review grants a raise; otherwise I'd keep the current household budget. Next spring I'd ask the union to bargain for a notice period and a published list of paid openings. In the first year after 2036, if my tax post ends, I'd take a funded co-op finance vacancy only with written mortgage-covering pay and a signed start; if none exists, I'd claim wage support and continue looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current thin savings, although a decade offers time. A long calendar is not an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on your children later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child would be nearly grown by then, but I don't want to put their wage in our mortgage plan. I'd rather build the reserve while Lina and I can work. The children should be free to leave home without a debt assignment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the union guarantee a new post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union can ask firms to publish funded posts, but it cannot create one by voting. If there is no opening, I keep any paid accounts hours and claim the support we qualify for. I would not spend savings on an unpaid placement.

say: I would seek **shared time** and paid training through a union agreement.
I would demand a **published list** of funded openings before posts end.
think: My **returns** still face AGI in 2036 despite the longer runway.
The **thin reserve** already threatens our family when two bills coincide.
do: Save **fifty monthly** only after a written raise.
Ask the **union** for notice and published paid openings.
After **2036 tax loss**, take funded mortgage-covering work with written start; otherwise claim support and keep searching.
feel: I feel **anxious** about thin savings now.
S4.quote: A long calendar is not an emergency fund.
fieldNote: The **raise condition** prevents a fictional savings path from low current pay.
His **2036 fallback** keeps paid hours and searches posted work if no co-op vacancy exists.

steps.text: Deposit fifty monthly only after firm grants written raise
Ask union to bargain for notice and published paid vacancies
Take funded co-op post after 2036 loss if written mortgage wage and start fit
Keep available paid accounts; seek eligible support and posted work after 2036 loss without vacancy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My tax desk could end before our family has a month of cash, and Lina's rota cannot cover the mortgage alone. Written notice, a temporary wage bridge, paid redeployment and a real funded post would help. A title at work is not an emergency fund at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the savings when a return takes half as long. The partners may see a better margin while my team sees a frozen vacancy. I want the client, the staff and the owners to see the same figures.

headlineQuote: A title at work is not an emergency fund at home.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Aaron leads three accountants preparing co-op accounts and tax returns.
His **master’s** and chartered qualification support top skill, while pay remains low.
He **never uses AI**, relying on human review and pressing the union for a voice.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and less than one month saved keep baseline worry high.
Few **nearby firms** limit escape, so he tests paid client demand and funded vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his screen work before the household builds a month of cash.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, temporary wages, paid redeployment and a funded post.
